newsitem.title: USA: World chemical weapons ban gets Republican backing.
newsitem.headline: World chemical weapons ban gets Republican backing.

text.p: A world treaty outlawing chemical weapons was assured of easy approval by the U.S. Senate on Thursday after Republican Leader Trent Lott dropped his opposition, paving the way for U.S. ratification.
Senators voted to strip a "killer" amendment from the resolution of ratification that would have prevented the United States from joining the Chemical Weapons Convention.
Votes were later taking place on four other amendments, three of which were regarded as killers, before the final vote on consenting to ratification took place on Thursday evening.
Lott told reporters he expected the treaty to be approved by a margin of 72 to 78 votes, in excess of the two-thirds majority needed for Senate passage.

The 1993 treaty aims to ban the production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons worldwide. More than 70 nations have already ratified the treaty, which goes into effect next Tuesday, with or without the United States.

Senate approval will allow President Bill Clinton to ratify the treaty before it comes into effect on Tuesday. Only the Senate is required to approve treaties, though both the Senate and the House will have to pass implementing legislation.
The first vote showed 26 Republicans joining all 45 Democrats to strip an amendment that would have conditioned U.S. ratification on so-called rogue nations joining the treaty.
Lott's change of stance was critical in obtaining the backing of undecided Republicans.

A crucial factor in Lott's support for the treaty was an 11th-hour letter from Clinton pledging to withdraw from it if other countries used its provisions to proliferate poison gas technology and endanger U.S. security.

Approval of the pact would be a major victory for Clinton, who has invested much political capital in a high-profile lobbying campaign. It included a White House ceremony on Wednesday at which his 1996 presidential election opponent, Bob Dole, endorsed the treaty, reversing earlier opposition.

Clinton's letter, released by Lott, eased concerns over treaty provisions requiring parties to provide chemical weapons defences and calling for exchanges of peaceful chemicals and technology between nations. Lott had voiced fears these provisions could be used by some countries to spread poison gas technology to so-called rogue states.
Clinton set out three scenarios under which the United States would be prepared to withdraw from the treaty. They were:
-if the treaty provisions were used to justify providing chemical weapons defensive equipment to a party that would result in degrading U.S. chemical defences;
-if it was used to justify transfers that would end the ability of a group of nations known as the Australia Group to control chemical weapons proliferation;
-or, if transfers were made under the pact that jeopardised U.S. security by promoting chemical weapons proliferation.

Other amendments that treaty supporters will seek to strip from the resolution would make U.S. ratification conditional on ratification by Russia, require striking out two treaty provisions addressed in Clinton's letter and set standards of verification against cheating that could not be met.
